Crystal structures and X-ray reference powder diffraction patterns have been determined for the Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 3, 4, 5, 7) series. Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 crystallize in the cubic perovskite structure with a space group Pm3 m (No. 221) and the lattice parameter increasing from a ¼ 4.08732(3) Å to a ¼ 4.08894 (2) Å as x varies from 1 to 7. The Goldschmidt distortion parameter for the entire series is about 1.05 (1.0488e1.0506), being similar to that of the cubic end member Ba3Nb2CoO9. Transmission electron microscopy of the composition Ba12Nb4Ta4Co4O36 (or Ba3(NbTaCo)O9) revealed nanoscale 1:2 ordering of Nb/Ta and Co, manifested in the presence of the diffuse superlattice reﬂections. As this ordering is limited to short range, the average structures were still reﬁned assuming the ideal-perovskite cubic symmetry. X-ray powder diffraction patterns of the studied compounds have been submitted to the Powder Diffraction File (PDF). © 2017 Elsevier Masson SAS. All rights reserved.

## 1. Introduction

Continuing demand for environmentally friendly alternative energy technologies motivates intense research in energy conversion. The efﬁciency and performance of thermoelectric energy conversion or cooling is related to the dimensionless ﬁgure of merit (ZT) of the thermoelectric (TE) materials, given by ZT ¼ S2sT/k, where T is the absolute temperature, S is the Seebeck coefﬁcient or thermoelectric power, s is the electrical conductivity, and k is the thermal conductivity [1]. Low dimensional, layered oxides exhibit relatively high efﬁciencies for high-temperature waste-heat conversion applications. Examples of these oxides include cobaltates, such as NaCoOx [2], Ca2Co3O6 [3,4], Ca3Co4O9 [5e9], Bi2Sr2Co2Ox [10] and Bi1-xPbxOCuSe [11]. Thus, considerable research has been conducted to study various cobaltates for thermoelectric applications, including phase diagram studies of ternary oxide systems with CaO and Co3O4 as two of the end members [12e15]. Perovskite oxides, which a general formula ABO3, have also attracted increasing attention in recent years as potential candidates for thermoelectric applications [16]. A number of these materials show reasonably high values of power factors. Perovskites

are distinguished by their ability to simultaneously accommodate a wide range of species on both 12-fold coordinated A and 6-fold B cation sites. A mismatch between ionic sizes and radii for the cations sharing the same crystallographic sites provides a driving force for the ordering of these species. Common examples of ordered arrangements for the B cations correspond to the general stoichiometries A2BB’O6 and A3B2B’O9 [17,18], which have been studied extensively. For example, Jacobson et al. [19] studied the series of Ba3B5þ2B02þO9, where B¼Ta and Nb, B’ ¼ Mg, Ni, Co, Zn, Mn, Ca, Sr, and Ba. However, they found that when B’ ¼ Ni, Co and Zn, the compounds remain disordered. The present paper has two goals. First, the structures of Ba12Nb8-

xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 2, 4, 5, 7) compounds are investigated for the effects of ionic size difference between Ta5þ and Nb5þ. Additionally, the X-ray diffraction patterns for Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 2, 4, 5, 7) are measured to make them widely available as references through submission to the Powder Diffraction File (PDF [20,21]).

The starting powders were mixed, pelletized, and calcined in air at 850 C for 12 h, followed by subsequent annealing at 950 C for 12 h, and at 1100 C for a total of 44 h with intermediate grindings. During each heat treatment, the samples were furnace cooled. The heat treatment process was repeated until no further changes were detected in the powder X-ray diffraction patterns.

2.2. X-ray rietveld reﬁnements and powder reference patterns1

The Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 3, 4, 5, 7) compounds were mounted as ethanol slurries on a zero-background cell. The X-ray diffraction powder patterns were measured using a Bruker D2 Phaser diffractometer (30 kV,10 mA, 5e130 2q in 0.024 steps,1 s/ step) equipped with a LynxEye position-sensitive detector. For all samples, the lower window of the detector electronics was increased from its default value of 0.11 Ve0.19 V to minimize the effects of ﬂuorescence. All patterns (especially those from the sintered disks) show evidence of granularity. The Rietveld reﬁnement technique [22] with the software suite GSAS [23] was used to determine the structure of Ba12Nb8-

xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 3, 4, 5, 7). Reference patterns were obtained using a Rietveld pattern decomposition technique. The reported peak positions were derived from the extracted integrated intensities, and positions calculated from the lattice parameters. For peaks that cannot be resolved, the intensities are summed, and an intensity-weighted d-spacing is reported.

2.3. Bond valence sum (BVS) calculations

The bond valence sum (BVS) values for the Ba, Nb, Ta, and Co sites were calculated using the Brown-Altermatt empirical expression [24,25]. The BVS of an atom i is deﬁned as the sum of the bond valences vij of all the bonds from atoms i to atoms j. The most commonly adopted empirical expression for the bond valence vij as a function of the interatomic distance dij is vij ¼ exp[(R0 - dij)/B]. The parameter, B, is commonly assumed to be a “universal” constant equal to 0.37 Å. The values for the reference distances R0 for Ba-O, Ta5þ-O, Nb5þ-O, Co2þ-O are (2.29, 1.920, 1.911, 1.692), respectively [24,25]. For crystallographic sites occupied by several types of atoms, the resulting BVS is calculated as the weighted sum according to site occupancies for the individual species.

2.4. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)

TEM samples were prepared by crushing the powder in ethanol and dispersing the resulting suspensions on lacey-carbon-coated copper grids. The samples were examined in a Philips CM30 TEM operated at 200 kV.

3.1. X-ray diffraction study

The results of Rietveld reﬁnement for the Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 2, 4, 5, 7) series are shown in Table 1 and Fig. 1. Table 1 gives various reﬁnement statistical agreement factors whereas in Fig. 1, the observed (crosses), calculated (solid line), and difference XRD patterns (bottom) for Ba12Nb4Ta4Co4O36 are illustrated; the difference pattern is plotted at the same scale. Above 60 2q, the vertical

The structures of the Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 3, 4, 5, 7) series are conﬁrmed to be cubic (ideal ABO3 perovskite), in agreement with previous reports by Jacobson et al. (1976). Table 2 lists the lattice parameters, which increase from a ¼ 4.08732(3) Å to 4.08894 (2) Å with increasing x. The apparent disorder of Nb, Ta, and Co observed for x  1 contrasts with the ordering of Nb and Co reported for the x ¼ 0 member of these series, Ba(Nb2/3Co1/3)O3 [26]. Fig. 2 illustrates changes in the unit-cell volumes, V, in Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 3, 4, 5, 7). V increases slightly (0.12%) across the entire solid solution series. Shannon [27] derived similar ionic radii of z0.64 Å for both Nb5þ and Ta5þ. Yet, recent evidence suggests that the effective radius of Ta is somewhat smaller than that of Nb. For example, measurements of extended X-ray absorption ﬁne structure (EXAFS) in Ag(Nb1/2Ta1/2)O3 [28] revealed that the Nb-O distance is 1.99(1) Å compared to 1.96 Å for the Ta-O pair. Keller and Kr€amer [29] have also suggested that Ta5þ has a slightly smaller ionic radius (by 0.007 Å) than that of Nb5þ.

3.2. TEM results

Representative selected area electron diffraction in the 〈110〉 zone-axis orientation is shown in Fig. 3. The strong reﬂections are indexed according to the ideal cubic perovskite unit cell. The pattern reveals additional diffuse reﬂections at g ¼ 1/3 [111]*

(asterisk refers to a reciprocal space), which are indicative of shortrange 1:2 ordering of Nb/Ta and Co on the octahedral sites, consistent with previous studies of BaCo1/3Nb2/3O3. Two twinvariants having the ordering vectors aligned with the [111] and [11-1] directions contribute to the pattern. Dark-ﬁeld imaging using these diffuse spots was challenging because of their weak intensity. However, considering the ﬁrst-order nature of the disorder-1:2 order transition and judging from the diffuse streaking, the sample likely features nanoscale precipitates of the ordered phase having their habit planes perpendicular to the ordering vector, as has been observed previously in related systems. The pattern also seems to feature the diffuse blobs of intensity at ½[111]*, which appear broader than might be expected from simple intersections of the diffuse streaks passing through 1/3[111]* reﬂections. These diffuse spots at ½[111]* could reﬂect the presence of 1:1 (rocksalttype) ordered regions along with those exhibiting 1:2 order. Such coexistence of 1:1 and 1:2 ordered regions has been reported for the structurally-related Ca4Nb2O9-CaTiO3 system [30]. Highresolution TEM imaging is necessary to identity the exact nature of the ½[111]* diffuse maxima. As the cation order in these present samples is limited to short range, the ideal-perovskite cubic Pm3m symmetry is used to describe the average structure of the Ba12Nb8-

xTaxCo4O36 series.

In these patterns, the symbols 'M0 and 'þ' refer to peaks containing contributions from two and more than two overlapping reﬂections, respectively. In general, the d-spacing values are calculated from reﬁned lattice parameters. The intensity values reported are integrated intensities

For resolved overlapped peaks, intensity-weighted calculated d-spacing, along with the observed integrated intensity and the hkl indices of both peaks (for ‘M’), or the hkl indices of the strongest peak (for ‘þ’) are used. In the case of a cluster, unconstrained proﬁle ﬁts often reveal the presence of multiple peaks, even when they are closer than the instrumental resolution. ## 4. Summary

Crystal structures and reference patterns of the Ba12Nb8-

xTaxCo4O36 (x ¼ 1, 2, 4, 5, 7) series of compounds have been determined and submitted to the Powder Diffraction File (PDF). According to X-ray powder diffraction, Ba12Nb8-xTaxCo4O36 adopts a simple perovskite structure. All the Ba sites have 12-fold coordination environment and all the mixed Co/Nb/Ta sites are 6-fold (octahedral) coordinated. TEM analysis of the Ba3(NbTaCo)O9 phase revealed short-range 1:2 ordering of Nb/Ta and Co on the octahedral sites. The slight changes in lattice parameters and the (Nb,Ta,Co)-O distances across the series might be related to the local cation ordering. The BVS values for the Ba sites (range from 2.172 to 2.166) indicate that the coordination environment around the large A site (in ABO3 perovskite structure) is slightly compressive. # Model Checking for Flexible Network Protocols

Andrew Johnson1(B ) , Dennis Fetterly2,  Sean  Song2 , and Jonathan Zolla2

1 Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA aj3189@princeton.edu 2 Google, Inc., Moun tain View, CA 94043, USA flexible-network-protocols-cav@google.com

Abstract. Operating a network is a daunting task. Operating one at a global scale, with stringent service objectives and requirements to be available during maintenance and failures, is even more so. At Google, we operate such a network. This paper details our experience applying formal methods to some of the networking protocols that are developed and maintained by in-house engineers. These protocols centrally route network traﬃc to respond to changes in demand, react to network failures, and allow for maintenance and upgrades. We used formal methods to target a class of bugs stemming from unclear speciﬁcations, unintended system interactions, and logical errors at the speciﬁcation level. We show how we modeled our protocols using an oﬀ-the-shelf model checker and a custom harness to scale the model horizontally. We were able to recreate several recent bugs and verify that the ﬁxes implemented were correct. Finally, we present a method called state projection that we used to increase conﬁdence in the coverage of our models, which we added to the TLC model checker for TLA+. We created 7 diﬀerent TLA+ models and showed that they were eﬀective at recreating bugs and verifying our ﬁxes to those bugs.

## 1 Introduction

Google operates B4, one of the largest privately operated netwo rks in the world [11,12], with stringent requirements for availability, bandwidth, and connectivity. It is managed with internally-developed control plane protocols for centralized traﬃc engineering, automatic failure recovery, and operator-initiated changes. A global scale and rapidly changing demand in response to traﬃc patterns or business needs stretch the network to operate in virtually every conceivable edge case. Furthermore, they are frequently updated. Engineers are able to ﬁx bugs, add features, and rework the protocols with a release time of weeks to months; in contrast, changes to public internet protocols require coordination between many stakeholders, taking years and requiring backwards-compatibility.

Control-plane protocols for B4 work at the abstraction level of sites,  which are composed of control domains that contain physical network devices. Traﬃc

We modeled the installation of a TED on individual domains using TLA+ (Temporal Logic of Actions), a formal speciﬁcation language [14,25]. TLA+ can be used to test safety properties, e.g. “Traﬃc never blackholes” or liveness properties, e.g. “TE Ops are eventually successful.” A TLA+ model has constants, variables (the program state), an initial state formula, and a transition relation. TLA+ speciﬁcations can be used as mathematically precise documentation and as input to TLC [14], which is an explicit-state model checker for TLA+ models.

TLC was not able to handle our use case immediately. Including enough detail from our protocols to reproduce simple bugs became infeasible. The tool does not scale well horizontally because it must maintain a global set of previously seen states. Instead, we developed a way to split the protocol into distinct phases and horizontally parallelize our model by input (network topology and desired TED). This allowed us t o run many instances of TLC which, when combined, explore the entire state space of the protocol. It also allowed us to perform symmetry reduction on the network topology, saving redundant work [5]. Finally, our production topology is too large for any model checker. Instead, we designed abstract interpretation-based summaries of the safety-critical portions of a state called state projections which provide a coverage criterion for exploration.

## 2 Model Description

The scope of our model is TED installation: TE Op generation, dependency computation, and installation order, as well as domain failure and recovery. We do not model the desired TED computation [11], instead assuming an optimal TED is given as input. We also do not model link failure and r ecovery, and exclude any transient network changes.

Constants. The speciﬁcs of the network topology are constants. This includes the sets of sites and d omains, as well as the relationships between them.

Variables. In TLA+, variables are the primary drivers of exploration time, as they deﬁne the criteria for a unique state. Our model includes these variables:

1. Desired TED: The current desired TED 2. Domain TEDs: Map from domains to their current TED 3. Domain Status: Map from domains to their status 4. CurrOps: Ops that have yet t o be complete 5. OpDependencies: Pairs of ops indicating a partial order of dependencies

Actions. Actions deﬁne the transition relation for a model. Ours has the following:

1. ComputeOps: Computes CurrOps (the diﬀerence between each Domain’s initial TED and the desired TED) and OpDependencies. The calculation of the OpDependencies caused many of our targeted historical bugs. Example dependencies include requiring tunnels to be installed on all domains before ﬂows that use them, or conversely removing a ﬂo w that uses a tunnel from all domains before removing the tunnel. Dependency computation also takes into account whether domains are FailOpen or NotReady. 2. InstallOp: The model can install any Op from CurrOps which does not depend on an incomplete Op and for which the domain is OK (a failed d omain would result in a failed Op). We model all possible Op interleavings. 3. DomainStatusChange: Domains can fail or recover at any time. Many bugs arose from dependencies on failed domains. When a domain fails, it immediately changes its status to FailOpen. Then, it creates an Op (and updates dependencies) to change its status to NotReady, since this must be comm unicated from the central controller to neighboring domains. Similarly, a domain returning to OK status creates an Op to mark it Ready. 4. ComputeTED: At the end of each round, compute a new TED to install.

Once there are no more ops, the round is complete and we nondeterministically choose a new desired TED for the next round. ## 3 Modeling Experience

Our process was to choose a past bug and create a TLA+ model that was as simple as possible while exhibiting the bug. Then, we implemented the bug’s ﬁx in the model and veriﬁed that the bug no longer appeared. We wished to model our protocols at a high enough ﬁdelity to catch bugs and reﬂect the actual structure of our code. The further abstracted our models are from the implementation, the more likely mistakes become when translating any protocol changes into the model, causing spurious errors or missing edge cases.

We quickly ran into the scaling problem inherent to explicit-state model checking. B4 has hundreds of domains and thousands of ﬂows and tunnels. At the ﬁdelity we desired, model checking any topology with more than a few nodes and tunnels was infeasible. In this section, w e describe how we built our model to take advantage of compute to scale short (single-round) runs out horizontally while giving us conﬁdence for long (multi-round) runs.

### 3.1 Single-Round Model

The example from Sect. 2 describes a protocol with many rounds of TE updates, which we call the Tunnel Install (TI) Linear model. A round begins when a new desired TED is decided and ends when all of the TE Ops have either completed or failed. Once we added any more complexity, this became infeasible because it was not only testing op interleavings within rounds, but also all possible interleavings of desired TEDs. Instead, we mo del a single round, and then check every possible single-round run of the model, which we call the TI model. The TI and TI Linear models are equivalent in the states they explore, as we show in Sect. 5.

Instead of generating a new TED at the end of each round, the TI model changes the desired TED from a variable to a constant. We also add a new constant, which determines all the possible starting TEDs. This simulates all possible states the multi-round mo del could be in when the ComputeTED action ends the round. Each TED becomes a distinct starting state so that we do not miss states that would arise from rounds ending with incomplete ops.

To scale horizontally, we wrote a test harness in Python that enumerates all possible desired TEDs to use as input constants. We performed symmetry reduction on most topology elements at this stage to reduce duplicate work. For each desired TED generated after performing symmetry reduction, we run the model from every possible starting conﬁguration of domain TEDs. The result is

## 4 Projected States

It is impossible to run our model with a topology at the size of our production network. To increase conﬁdence that our models have enough coverage on small topologies, we compute succinct, topology-agnostic abstractions of concrete states, which we call state projections. Intuitively, small topologies are “big enough” because, in our protocols, tunnels and ﬂows are independent of one another and tunnel length does not m atter. We are completing an exhaustive state space exploration, so we will explore every possible state that a short tunnel can reach, and the states of a long tunnel will be variations on that theme.

TLC uses hash ﬁngerprints to keep track of previously seen states. We modiﬁed TLC to include another ﬁngerprint for the state projection. Projections should be topology-agnostic; that is, the set of possible projections should be the same no matter the topology. Formally, a TLA+ model has a (possibly inﬁ- nite) concrete state space S and a ﬁnite projected state space A. The state projection, α, has domain S and range \mathcal{P}(P(A)) (the set of subsets of A). This is most similar to classical predicate abstraction [2,6,9]. However, each concrete state maps to a set of per-domain summaries, making projections simpler to express. In our example model from Sect. 2, we deﬁne a projection a s follows:

Deﬁnition 3. A domain projection of a domain dd and tunnel tt is a tuple containing the following:

1. The domain’s state, either OKOK or FailOpenFailOpen 2. The domain’s global status, either ReadyReady or NotReadyNotReady. 3. A boolean indicating whether or not tt is used at domain dd. 4. A boolean indicating whether or not tt is installed a t dd.

The projection of a concrete state ss is the set of domain projections for any c ombination of domain and tunnel.

This projection summarizes the safety-relevant state of each domain. The domain projection is enough to tell whether a domain is blackholing: a domain must be ready and used by a tunnel that is not installed. It is topology-agnostic as it does not scale with the numbe r of domains or tunnels (there are 16 possible projections). This projection is hand-crafted, but is relatively clear from the system design. We verify in Sect. 6 that our models visit a state with every safe domain projection, and use this as a proxy for the coverage of our models. This does not provide a proof that no additional projected states can be discovered after a plateau, called stuttering. To provide such a proof, one w ould need to create an abstract program that operates over sets of projected states, or ﬁnd another way to rule out stuttering behavior, such as with resource-unbounded analysis [13,15,16].

## 5 Evaluation

In evaluating our approach, we asked the following questions:

1. Did our models scale enough to give us conﬁdence we are not missing bugs? 2. Were we able to complete model checking i n a reasonable amount of time? 3. Did our single-round optimization of the tunnel installation protocol explore all t he same states as the linear one?

### 5.1 Setup

We created the following mo dels for testing:

1. Tunnel Install (TI) Linear: The model described in Sect. 2. 2. TI: The model described in Sect. 3.1. 3. TI NoFail: The same as TI, but without domain failure or recovery. 4. TI Groups (TI+G): This model adds the concept of Tunnel Groups to TI. Groups spread large ﬂows across multiple tunnels, which may take diﬀerent paths. This was required to recreate a bug which allowed tunnels to be added to groups before they were fully installed. 5. TI+G NoFail: The same as TI+G, but without domain failure or recovery. 6. Domain Drain: This is the network protocol used by the control plane to “drain” a domain, meaning moving traﬃc away from it. It is modeled at the same abstraction level as the Tunnel Install models, and is the implementation of the step in t hose models that changes a domain to or from “Ready”. We used a projection that tracks a domain’s status, readiness status, and the status of its connected external links. 7. Local Drain: This is the protocol used to drain a single network device within a domain. It is modeled at the level of a single domain. We used a projection that tracks a domain’s status and the status of its connected external links.

We chose 5 sample topologies that all of the models were able to ﬁnish exploring, starting from the simplest possible and increasing in complexity. For example, with the TI models, topology 1 has two nodes and one tunnel and ﬂow, while topology 5 has six nodes with two tunnels and two ﬂows. They are equivalent up to diﬀerences required for the diﬀerent models (e.g. the addition of tunnel groups). For each model, we wrote a Python test harness to determine all possible desired TEDs and initial states for a topology, up to symmetry reduction.

### 5.2 Results

We found that our models were able to scale past when the topology is big enough to saturate the (safe) projected state space. The two projected states left unexplored by all of the TI models are unsafe. For the models without domain failure, they never explore projected states with domain statuses other than (OK, Ready). For ones with domain failure, they explore these early and then plateau, exploring the same projected states with much larger topologies.

We also found that with the single-round model checking approach, our models all complete in a reasonable amount of time. The largest topology with the most complex model (TI+G with failure) takes less than an hour. Most complete in less than a minute. This is fast enough to be run repeatedly while updating the model. We had outlier topologies for the single-round approach (the max time was much greater than the average) due to combinatorial explosion in the initial state space for empty desired TEDs. We also created a linear model with groups, but it became infeasible for all but the smallest topology, which is evidence that our approach scales better than the linear one.

Finally, to verify that our single-round optimization does not miss states, we ran the TI model with no initial symmetry reduction alongside the TI Linear model. We had TLC dump the states for both and combined all of the dumped states from the single-round runs. Then, we veriﬁed that the single-round version explored the exact same states as the linear one by comparing the values of the variables in each state (excluding the additional variables required to track state across rounds). This was true for all of the TI Linear runs.

## 6 Discussion

Developer Eﬀort. We found TLA+ to have a steep but short learning curve. Once overcome, each model took a developer about one week to create while learning the speciﬁcs of the design. Developing and testing multiple iterations of the single-round versions, complete with Python harnesses and test scripts for use in Google’s Borg system took about two person-months, most of which produced reusable scaﬀolding. The “Drain” models (6 and 7) were created for future changes rather than previous bugs, and showed success with design-time modeling, as they helped ﬁnd multiple errors in early protocol proposals and forced engineers to write their protocol change and desired properties precisely. This saved signiﬁcant eﬀort when compared to implementing and testing the changes in a network simulator, which may not have caught the errors. We also experimented with liveness properties such a s verifying that all ops are eventually installed under diﬀerent fairness assumptions, but focused on the NoBlack- Holes safety property for the evaluation because it is equivalent between all of our examples. Finally, we found the single-round model useful in development because it was easy to run quickly (with limited starting states) while changing the protocol. It also made counterexamples easier to read than tracing a long, multi-round run.

Computational Cost. The primary challenge was ensuring our models ran eﬃ- ciently. There is an inherent tension with models that are not provably connected to the runtime system: on one hand, we wished to optimize the models for faster runtimes and bigger topologies. On the other hand, the further the model gets from the real system, the more “hand-waving” is required to be sure one is not fabricating bugs, or worse, missing them. We needed a high level of abstraction in order to get something diﬀerent from a network simulator for testing, which is already done extensively on all B4 changes.

Extensibility. We faced unique challenges in this project that depart from oneshot academic veriﬁcation projects, including the need for fast changes, a global scale, and a long list of speciﬁc problems to target. W e think two main takeaways are useful for developers wishing to apply similar methods.

First, the “single-round” approach was successful because it gave a start and end to a reactive system, which was possible because the single TE process acted as a leader that deﬁned the rounds. We believe there are many problems in networking and other areas that have layers of abstraction where one can perform the “outer loop” in parallel to increase compute eﬃciency. For example, BGP could treat each route announcement as a “single round.” In networking speciﬁcally, control plane protocols are a good match for model checking because they are insulated by well-deﬁned abstraction layers from concerns like individual packets and physical links. It also allowed us to perform symmetry reduction at the example level with symmetries that could not be applied at the level of a ﬁxed model. Since there was no single state set, the number of diﬀerent conﬁgurations could be very large and we were able to run dozens of jobs in parallel.

Second, pen-and-paper design documents were a useful level of abstraction for formal modeling. They are early enough in the development process to catch bugs before incurring the cost of bringing a change to a testable state. Google employs a wide variety of network testing sc hemes, but all require a change to be designed and at least partially implemented, whereas model-checking is able to ﬁnd errors at the pseudo-code level.

Limitations. We left as out of scope errors that occur between the network devices and domain controllers, as well as a host of other concerns such as the mechanics of retransmitted messages, hardware malfunctions other than total failures, and bugs in unmodeled systems. We also do not model every piece of the protocol, instead choosing to simplify models as much as possible while still recreating real-world bugs. A monolithic model w ould be infeasible for model checking, so we hope to have a range of simpliﬁed models (about one per design document) to allow engineers to choose the best abstraction level.

The single-round method improves performance, but still suﬀers from combinatorial explosion. Techniques for sharing the ﬁngerprint state set a cross parallel computations, such as those developed for DiVinE [3], could aid in reducing repeated work. We found our approach to scale better than the distributed mode of TLC, which also cannot check liveness properties. Furthermore, for very large topologies, generating (and symmetry reducing) possible conﬁgurations could also suﬀer, though this might be avoided with better reduction techniques [7].

Currently, temporal formulas cannot be included in state projections. While it was not required for our models, this would be an interesting avenue for future work and would allow for more complex projections. We would also like to close the Abstract Interpretation loop for projected states by developing a way to compute an abstract program from a T LA+ model. This could be especially challenging if temporal formulas were added to projections, but would give a veriﬁcation procedure for topologies of any size.

## 7 Related Work

There is a wide range of network veriﬁcation systems that have been developed, each with diﬀerent tradeoﬀs of user eﬀort to guarantee strength. On one end of the spectrum are systems such as IronFleet, Verdi, I vy, I4, Minesweeper, CCAC, and TimePiece, which all focus on ﬁnding strong inductive invariants of distributed systems [1,10,17,22,27]. Because they require signiﬁcant dedicated user eﬀort, they are meant for widely-used systems such as public-internet protocols or consensus protocols. A similar large, one-time eﬀort to formalize and verify Google’s algorithms would be diﬃcult to maintain across protocol changes. Eﬀorts to lower this cost such as DistAI, which attempts to automatically generate invariants, and Grove, which employs separation logic to modularize proofs, still require protocol speciﬁcations in a proof language [23,28]. A model-checking approach makes the most sense for our use case, as model complexity matches the level of design documentation and changes will be similar and proportional to implementation changes.

Symmetry reduction has been used in many forms to tackle state space explosion, for example in hardware veriﬁcation [19], parameterized systems [4,8], and symbolic model checking [7,20]. These approaches provide strong theoretical guarantees but would require implementation in TLC. The best available tools are TLC’s reﬁnement checker or Apalache [21], which still require the user to provide the entire abstract program in addition to the abstraction. State projections are a practical s tarting point for deﬁning abstractions without symbolic execution or BDD machinery.

In contrast to proof-based systems, network runtime veriﬁcation systems such as Aragog or Pivot Tracing are automated but incur a runtime cost a nd only check events that they observe directly [18,29]. Google already uses runtime veriﬁcation extensively. Our approach is in the middle: it can ﬁnd bugs at the level of design documents, is easy to set up and modify as it d oes not touch the production system, and does not require modeling the entirety of the network.

## 8 Conclusion

We presented our experience using TLA+ to model some of the control plane protocols running on Google’s B4. We modeled various protocols at a high level of abstraction akin to a design document. To perform model checking on them, we present a novel technique to horizontally parallelize model checking in our speciﬁc domain. Furthermore, we added an abstraction mechanism to TLA+ to ensure we explored all abstract states of interest to developers. We evaluated our techniques on various network topologies and showed that they made the model checking problem feasible.
